newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Bonds on stocks, dollar watch.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Bonds on stocks, dollar watch.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury market gets two items of economic news on Friday but the thought that will dominate it in its first hours of trading on Friday is whether stocks will continue their Thursday selloff.
The stock market plunged in late trade on Thursday, losing nearly 100 points in its biggest point-loss since mid-July and it followed a drop of 71 points on Wednesday.
"Traders will be keenly interested in how the stock market plays out," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A.
"If there's more selling in stocks, the bill market gets richer (on flight to quality buying) and it helps the long bond (yield) hold support at 6-5/8 percent, at least temporarily," said Stiles.
Bond prices ended slightly higher on Thursday and bill rates fell. The 6-1/2 percent 30-year bond yield finished at 6.62 percent.
"The market already has a bid at the short end (because of the stock selloff)," observed Matthew Alexy, chief markets strategist at CS First Boston. "The curve will steepen out."
The spread between the two- and 30-year yields finished at 83 basis points on Thursday.
Alexy said bond prices could hold up if the stock market slides again on Friday because "we're getting very close to fair value in bonds."
But if the dollar breaks down in addition to stocks, the bond story could be different, he said.
"If foreigners are selling U.S. stocks, then the dollar will go down and bonds will go down with it," said Alexy.
Alexy said bonds are trading very technically and "price action, not value, is forcing investment decisions right now."
Support for T-bonds lies at 112-10 on the March futures contract, said Alexy.
"If that breaks, we go right up to a (30-year bond) yield of 6.74 percent," he said.
Alexy said resistance probably lies at 114 even on the March contract.
As the year draws to a close, players are on the defensive, he said.
"There are buying opportunities that are not being taken advantage of because of the time of year," he said. "People don't want to lose money in the last two weeks of the year.
"You won't put on a new position if you're afraid it will go under water, even if it's cheap," he said. "If you have a position with a profit, you want to take that profit and defend it."

The economic data the market gets on Friday -- October business inventories and the University of Michigan preliminary December consumer sentiment survey -- are scheduled for release at 1000 EST/1500 GMT.
Economists polled by Reuters look for a 0.2 percent increase in October business inventories after a 0.1 percent October rise.

"The inventory levels give an early hint on how the quarter is starting on the inventory side," said Stiles. "If inventories are higher than expected, then you would have to determine whether the buildup is voluntary -- caused by demand for products -- or involuntary."
The figure is not likely to be a market mover, he said.
"Business inventories is probably more of an economist's number than a trader's number," said Stiles.
The University of Michigan consumer sentiment survey -- forecast in a Reuters poll at 99.2 -- will attract interest.
"How the consumer finishes 1996 is of critical importance to the bond market," said Stiles.
-- North American Treasury Desk 212-859-1679
